title: Scams, Deception & Social Engineering
description: First unit: Time pressure and cognitive overload. Work through real situations, competing explanations and practical choices.

lessons.title: What is really happening?
lessons.teach: Alina receives a call claiming to be from her bank's fraud department. Rob is with her.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Listen closely to what each person says and what still remains uncertain.
nodes.explanation: Authority cues and urgency narrow the space for deliberation. A claimed emergency is used to make independent verification feel costly.
nodes.counterexample: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
nodes.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.
nodes.scenario: Alina receives a call claiming to be from her bank's fraud department. Rob is with her.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
An urgent message supposedly from a university asks a student to enter a password through a link before a scholarship offer expires.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Authority cues and urgency narrow the space for deliberation. A claimed emergency is used to make independent verification feel costly.

Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
